name: 戸隠流そば打ち処實徳 (Togakure-ryu Soba Uchidokoro Minori)

claims.text: This is a hand-cut soba shop, and the dough is made with Togakushi buckwheat at roughly 70% soba content, meaning the remaining portion is wheat flour (a two-to-eight / nihachi-style blend). The noodles are not gluten-free and the shop is not celiac-safe.

No gluten-free soba (such as a 100% buckwheat / juwari option) or any dedicated allergen preparation is indicated in available sources. Shared boiling water and a wheat-dusted work surface make cross-contamination likely; strictly gluten-intolerant diners should avoid.
Soba is served with a soy-sauce-based tsuyu/dashi. Japanese soy sauce typically contains wheat, so the dipping sauce is an additional source of gluten beyond the noodles themselves.

The tsuyu and dashi at a traditional soba shop are typically made with bonito (katsuobushi) and other fish-based stock, so even noodle-only dishes are generally not vegan. No vegan preparation is indicated.

Cold soba is offered served simply with salt, allowing the buckwheat's flavor to come through without the soy-based tsuyu, though this does not make the wheat-containing noodles safe for celiac diners.

name: とんかつ処 勝裕（かつひろ） (Tonkatsu-dokoro Katsuhiro)

claims.text: This is a tonkatsu specialist: cutlets are coated in wheat flour and wheat panko breadcrumbs and deep-fried, so the core menu is not gluten-free and is not safe for celiacs.

The kitchen fries a wide range of breaded items — pork loin and fillet cutlets, croquettes, fried shrimp, and oyster fry — in shared oil, so cross-contamination with wheat breading is effectively unavoidable.

Tonkatsu sauce contains wheat and soy, and the set meals come with miso soup (pork miso/tonjiru) and rice; miso and most Japanese soy sauce typically contain wheat, so seasonings and accompaniments add further gluten exposure.
There is no vegan or vegetarian offering: the menu is built on pork and seafood cutlets, the soup is a pork-based miso soup, and dashi/soy-based seasonings are used throughout.
This is not celiac-safe. The signature dish is a breaded, deep-fried pork cutlet (wheat flour and panko) served on bread, so gluten is central to almost everything here.
No gluten-free accommodation is indicated in any source, and the katsu is fried in shared oil with no mention of a dedicated fryer, so cross-contamination should be assumed.

The cutlets are heavily dipped in tonkatsu sauce, and the izakaya menu is sauce- and soy-based; most Japanese soy sauce and tonkatsu sauce contain wheat, so these are not safe for wheat or gluten avoidance.
The menu is built almost entirely around pork (tonkatsu, katsu sando, tonteki, salt-boiled pork) plus seafood and dashi-based izakaya dishes, with no vegan or vegetarian options indicated.
This is a tonkatsu specialist: the cutlets are pork coated in wheat-flour panko breadcrumbs and deep-fried, so the core dishes are not gluten-free and are not safe for celiac diners.
Frying is done in shared oil used for breaded, wheat-coated cutlets and minced cutlets, with no indication of a dedicated gluten-free fryer, so cross-contamination risk is high in this small kitchen.

The house-made tonkatsu sauce and the accompaniments (pickles, miso soup) typically contain wheat and/or soy; most Japanese soy sauce and sauce bases are brewed with wheat, so assume gluten is present throughout the meal.

This is a pork tonkatsu house; the menu centers on deep-fried pork cutlets, the soup is a pork-and-miso soup, and no vegetarian or vegan dishes are indicated. The kitchen is not suitable for vegan diners and cross-contact with animal products is unavoidable.

name: 和ダイニング なかぎし (Wa Dining Nakagishi)

claims.text: The entire menu is built around a single continuously-replenished dashi pot in which the oden — including the tofu, deep-fried tofu, yuba and vegetable items — is simmered alongside fish cakes (練り物) and other processed, soy- and wheat-containing ingredients, so there is no way to isolate a plain vegetable or tofu item from gluten and fish contact.
The kitchen also serves karaage and tempura, which are wheat-battered/floured fried foods; there is no indication of a dedicated gluten-free fryer or any allergen separation.

This is a soy- and dashi-driven oden/izakaya kitchen. The simmering broth and most preparations rely on soy sauce and dashi, and standard Japanese soy sauce contains wheat — the oden items themselves include fish cakes and processed (練り物) products that are typically made with wheat starch.

Even the vegetable and tofu oden items are cooked in a shared dashi that is fish- and bonito-based and topped up continuously, so vegetable items are not vegan. The broader menu is heavy on sashimi, seafood oden and meat.
A dish like the tofu okonomiyaki is specifically described as made with Japanese dashi broth, underscoring that even tofu/vegetable-forward plates carry animal-based dashi.

The master is known for being unusually warm and welcoming for Gion, including to first-time and solo visitors, so it is worth speaking to him directly about what you can and cannot eat — though no gluten-free or vegan accommodation is documented.

This is a soba shop whose core product is buckwheat noodles, and traditional soba is very commonly cut with wheat flour (nihachi, roughly 20% wheat). No gluten-free noodle or dedicated preparation is advertised, so the soba itself should be treated as containing wheat unless the shop confirms otherwise.

The kitchen also turns out tempura and breaded sauce katsudon, both wheat-based and deep-fried; the same boiling water, broth pots, and frying setup are shared across dishes, so cross-contamination with wheat is highly likely. Not celiac-safe.

The dipping/pouring tsuyu and dashi are soy-sauce based, and most Japanese soy sauce is brewed with wheat. The sauce on the sauce katsudon is likewise soy/wheat based. Assume the broths and sauces contain both wheat and soy.

The soba broth and dashi are bonito/fish based (oroshi soba is finished with katsuobushi), and the menu is built around pork katsudon and tempura, so vegan diners should confirm directly. Even a plain soba would normally sit in a fish-dashi tsuyu.

This is not a celiac-safe or gluten-free destination. The signature manbo-yaki and the okonomiyaki are built on a wheat-flour batter and combined with udon or soba noodles, so wheat is central to nearly every dish. The shared iron griddle, where batter, noodles, and other items are cooked together, makes cross-contamination effectively unavoidable.

Dishes are finished with okonomiyaki sauce (offered in sweet, sweet-and-spicy, or spicy versions), which is wheat- and soy-based, as is typical for this style. No wheat-free sauce option is indicated.

The menu is heavily meat- and seafood-based, with the signature dish layering beef tendon, oil cracklings, squid, offal, and egg, all cooked on a shared griddle. There is no indication of vegan options or separate preparation, so vegan diners should not rely on this restaurant.

This is a wheat-batter okonomiyaki shop cooked on a shared teppan (griddle), where noodles, batter, and multiple dishes are prepared on the same surface. It is not celiac-safe, and cross-contamination on the shared griddle is very likely. No gluten-free preparation is documented.
The signature dishes (manbo-yaki, beta-yaki, hoso-yaki) are built on a wheat-flour batter and frequently include wheat noodles (soba-iri).

The okonomiyaki sauce is described as sweet (or spicy) and is brushed on by the diner at the counter; this style of sauce is soy/Worcester-based and Japanese soy sauce typically contains wheat. Treat the sauce as containing gluten.

Not vegan-friendly. Dishes are dashi-heavy (bonito-based) and toppings center on pork, beef tendon, egg, and offal; finished with bonito flakes. No vegan preparation is documented and the shared teppan handles animal products throughout.
